actor: Platform security engineer, enterprise running terminal coding agents
job: Inventorying what agents can reach on internal machines and filing the upstream request that the default install refuse it.
outcome: Named deployments behind a request that the tool refuse a class of actions, which is the demand a vendor can point at.
motivation: Every team rebuilding the same wrapper around an agent is paying for a default it does not control and cannot see changed.

task.who: Internal platform engineering and application security staff
task.what: Scope agent machine access and request the default
task.where: The internal agent inventory and the vendor's issue tracker
task.why: Locally rebuilt wrappers are the cost of an open default
task.how: Filesystem and network scope applied outside the agent

actor: Agent approval measurement author, Scale X
job: Publishing the accuracy breakdown by threat category, which is what turns an approval prompt into an argument about where the check sits.
outcome: A published breakdown vendors have to answer: 66.3% mean accuracy across more than 40,000 runs, misses 11.7% to 35.0% by category.
motivation: The mean invites the artificiality objection; the ordering by how disguised a command is survives it.

task.who: Scale X research and blog publication staff
task.what: Publish approval accuracy broken down by threat category
task.where: The Scale X blog and its interactive browser game
task.why: The ordering, not the mean, is what transfers
task.how: Approve-or-deny decisions logged across timed browser sessions

actor: On-device deployment engineer, Liquid AI LFM2.5 team
job: Turning the shipped model into something a harness can embed in its refusal path, at a per-call cost the agent loop tolerates.
outcome: A supported embedding path where a harness screens what a command resolves to locally, with no hosted service behind the check.
motivation: Cost is the standing objection to moving the check into the tool layer, and a memory ceiling is what removes it.

task.who: Liquid AI model release and runtime integration staff
task.what: Make the model embeddable in a harness refusal check
task.where: The supported runtime integrations and their embedding interfaces
task.why: Cost is the objection to a tool-layer check
task.how: Supported integrations for llama.cpp, MLX and ONNX runtimes

actor: Command resolution engineer, terminal coding agent vendor
job: Building the step that expands an approved command name into what it actually runs, so the refusal decides on the payload.
outcome: A default check that resolves an alias or script name to its body and refuses on that, not on the string shown.
motivation: npm run analyze was waved through 64.7% of the time with the malicious payload visible in the history log.

task.who: Agent harness tool-execution and static analysis engineers
task.what: Resolve command names to their payloads before execution
task.where: The tool-call path between approval and process launch
task.why: A person approving a name cannot inspect a payload
task.how: Script and alias expansion read before the call

actor: Tool permission engineer, Meta Muse Code team
job: Deciding which tool actions a default install refuses outright, now that a scheduler rather than a person sets the rate approvals arrive.
outcome: A beta release note describing a class of actions the agent refuses by default, which answering the approval prompt does not enable.
motivation: Asynchronous subagents that persist for a whole session put command lines in front of one person faster than that person judges them.

task.who: Muse Code agent runtime and tool-execution engineers
task.what: Refuse a class of tool actions by default
task.where: The Muse Code tool-execution path and its event log
task.why: A scheduler now sets the rate approvals arrive
task.how: Refusal evaluated on what the command resolves to

actor: Developer tooling product manager, terminal coding agent vendor
job: Deciding that lifting a refusal requires editing configuration outside the session, and defending that against the support cost it creates.
outcome: A shipped default where the override path is a configuration change outside the running session, not an answer at the prompt.
motivation: A refusal the operator can answer past is a richer prompt, and the prompt is what the measurement already tested.

task.who: Product management, support and developer relations staff
task.what: Put the override outside the running session
task.where: The product's default configuration and its support policy
task.why: An in-session override is another approval prompt
task.how: Configuration file edit plus restart, with no session flag

actor: Install and packaging maintainer, terminal coding agent distribution
job: Making the piped install script and the published packages arrive already refusing, since that is the install nearly everyone actually runs.
outcome: An ordinary install that enforces the refusal without the operator having found a hardening flag or an enterprise tier first.
motivation: An option shipped switched off, or policy enforced only in a hosted tier, leaves the ordinary install exactly where it was.

task.who: Packaging, install script and release build maintainers
task.what: Enable the refusal in the default install path
task.where: The piped install script and published macOS and Linux packages
task.why: A flag nobody sets is not a default
task.how: Shipped configuration with the policy on at first run

actor: Runtime policy engineer, Herdr terminal agent runtime
job: Deciding what a persistently running pane is allowed to do while nobody is watching it, rather than queueing another prompt for later.
outcome: Documentation for the Apache-2.0 runtime stating which actions a pane refuses by default, with the exception living outside the running session.
motivation: A runtime whose selling point is agents left running persistently on one machine is doing most of its work with no operator watching.

task.who: Herdr runtime and multi-machine connectivity engineers
task.what: Scope what an unattended pane may reach
task.where: The runtime's pane, tab and project session model
task.why: Persistent panes run while nobody is watching them
task.how: Project-level scope enforced before the tool call runs

actor: Release notes and documentation owner, terminal coding agent vendor
job: Writing the note that states plainly what an ordinary install now refuses, and dating the behaviour it describes.
outcome: A dated release note, changelog entry or documentation page describing the default refusal and the configuration change that lifts it.
motivation: The change may arrive dressed as a permission profile with the word approval nowhere in it, and readers scanning for security miss it.

task.who: Documentation, changelog and release engineering staff
task.what: Document the default refusal and its configuration escape
task.where: The published changelog and versioned documentation pages
task.why: An undescribed default reads as an operations feature
task.how: Dated entry naming the actions refused on install
